sections.h: The book of Zephaniah in one page
sections.b: Zephaniah son of Cushi, a descendant of a Hezekiah four generations back, prophesied in the reign of Josiah (640 to 609 BC). His three chapters announce the day of the LORD against Judah and the whole earth (chapter 1), call the humble to seek the LORD and turn on Philistia, Moab and Ammon, Cush and Assyria (chapter 2), and then accuse Jerusalem, promise the nations pure lips and a humble remnant, and end with the LORD rejoicing over a rescued Daughter Zion (chapter 3).

common: The prophet worked in the early years of Josiah, before the reform of 622 BC, and the 'day' he announced was fulfilled by Babylon.
uncommon: Several critics think the closing hope (3:9-20) comes from the exile or later.

sections.h: Dies irae: Zephaniah 1:15 in the Latin hymn
sections.b: The Latin of Jerome's Vulgate at Zephaniah 1:15, dies irae, dies illa ("a day of wrath, that day"), opens the medieval sequence sung at funeral Masses. The hymn has been attributed to Thomas of Celano, a Franciscan of the 1200s, though the attribution is uncertain. It describes the last judgment with the trumpet, the book and the judge, and it has been set by Mozart, Verdi and many others. The 1969 reform of the funeral rite removed it as the Requiem sequence; the 1962 Missal keeps it, and the Liturgy of the Hours uses it divided into three hymns.

common: The hymn reads Zephaniah's day as the day of the last judgment, which the prophet's own text does not say.
uncommon: Some Protestant composers set the same words in funeral music without the Catholic prayers for the dead.

sections.b: "The army of the heavens" (tseva hashamayim) is the sun, moon and stars, thought of as living powers that march at the LORD's command. The Bible forbids bowing to them (Deuteronomy 4:19; 17:3), reports that Manasseh built altars to them in the Temple courts (2 Kings 21:3-5), that people burned incense to them on their roofs (Jeremiah 19:13; 32:29; Zephaniah 1:5), and that Josiah removed their priests and altars (2 Kings 23:4-5, 11-12). The "LORD of Armies" is the one who commands this army (Isaiah 40:26).

common: The cult grew under Manasseh and was Judean, not imposed by Assyria.
uncommon: Older scholarship held that Assyria forced its astral religion on its vassals.

sections.b: The Hebrew 'anawim ("the humble") and 'aniyyim ("the afflicted") name people who are low in power and who depend on God. Moses is called 'anav (Numbers 12:3). Psalm 37:11 says the humble will inherit the land. Zephaniah 2:3 calls the humble of the land to seek humility, and 3:12 says God will leave in Jerusalem "a people afflicted and poor" who take refuge in his name. Matthew 5:3-5, Luke 6:20 and Mary's song in Luke 1:46-55 draw on the same tradition. Scholars since Rahlfs (1892) and Gelin (1953) have spoken of "the poor of the LORD"; whether they were a party or only a spirit is debated.

common: The 'anawim' are those, rich or poor, who rely on God alone.
uncommon: Some see a distinct pious group in post-exilic Judah who wrote many of the psalms.

sections.b: Zephaniah 1:7-18 is the fullest single description of the day: a sacrifice with invited guests (1:7), a search with lamps (1:12), and a day of fury, darkness, the ram's horn and the battle cry (1:14-16). Silver and gold cannot buy anyone out (1:18). The book returns to it in 2:2-3, where the humble might be hidden "on the day of the LORD's anger," and in 3:8, where the whole earth is eaten up in the fire of God's jealousy. The Latin of 1:15 gave the church the hymn Dies irae.

In Zephaniah the remnant is the humble: "a people afflicted and poor" who take refuge in the LORD's name, do no wrong, speak no lies and lie down without fear (3:12-13). Judah's remnant also takes over the Philistine coast (2:7) and plunders Moab and Ammon (2:9). The book uses the words "what is left of Baal" (1:4) for the opposite remnant, which is cut off.

The heading puts Zephaniah "in the days of Josiah son of Amon." The idolatry he lists (Baal, idol priests, roof worship, Milcom) is the idolatry Josiah removed in 2 Kings 23:4-14, and most scholars place the prophecy before the reform of 622 BC. Huldah, the prophet whom Josiah's officials consulted, lived in "the second district" of Jerusalem (2 Kings 22:14), which Zephaniah names in 1:10. Jeremiah began to prophesy in the same reign (Jeremiah 1:2).

sections.h: Mixing the worship of the LORD with other gods
sections.b: Zephaniah 1:5 names people who bow down and swear oaths to the LORD and also swear by Milcom. This is syncretism, a blend. It is the sin the prophets attack most often: not forgetting the LORD, but making him one among several. Amos 8:14 and Jeremiah 5:7 make the same charge.

Zephaniah 1:4 promises to cut off "what is left of Baal" (the Greek has "the names of Baal") from Jerusalem. After Manasseh's altars to Baal (2 Kings 21:3) and Josiah's purge (2 Kings 23:4-5), the phrase suggests that some of the cult had survived into Josiah's early years.

Zephaniah 1:5 names Milcom, the god of Ammon, as one of the gods sworn by in Jerusalem. Zephaniah 2:8-11 then turns on the Ammonites and Moabites themselves, who insulted God's people and will become "like Sodom" and "like Gomorrah." Both peoples traced their ancestry to Lot (Genesis 19:36-38).
sections.refs: Zephaniah 1:5; Zephaniah 2:8-11; Genesis 19:36-38; 1 Kings 11:5; 2 Kings 23:13; Jeremiah 49:1-6

sections.b: Moab's insults against Judah are answered in Zephaniah 2:8-11: Moab will be "like Sodom," a place of nettles and a pit of salt, and the remnant of Judah will plunder it. Whether these insults are from Josiah's time or the fall of Jerusalem is debated.

Zephaniah 2:4-7 names four of the five Philistine cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron) and the Kerethites. The Hebrew plays on the names: "Gaza will be abandoned," "Ekron will be uprooted." Ashdod fell after a long siege by Egypt (Herodotus 2.157); Ashkelon was destroyed by Babylon in 604 BC (Babylonian Chronicle; excavations at Ashkelon).

Cush appears three times in Zephaniah: the prophet's father is Cushi (1:1), the Cushites fall by the LORD's sword (2:12), and from beyond the rivers of Cush worshipers bring offerings (3:10). The same people are slain and then bring a gift: the book's picture of the nations goes both ways.

sections.h: The end of Assyria in Zephaniah
sections.b: Zephaniah 2:13-15 announces that the LORD will "wipe out Assyria" and make Nineveh a ruin dry as the desert. Nineveh fell in 612 BC to the Babylonians and Medes; Ashur-uballit II held out at Harran until about 609. If the oracle was spoken in Josiah's early years, it was a bold word against the world power of the day.

Zephaniah's Nineveh is the city that exulted and sat secure, that said "I am, and besides me there is nothing" (2:15), the same boast Babylon makes in Isaiah 47:8. It becomes a lair for desert owls and hedgehogs with a voice singing from the window. Nahum shows the city's fall in full; Jonah shows the city's repentance.

Zephaniah 1:10-11 names three places in Jerusalem: the Fish Gate in the north wall, the Second District (hamishneh, where Huldah lived) and the Mortar (hammakhtesh, a market). Chapter 3 then calls the city "rebellious and defiled" (3:1) and, in the end, "Daughter Zion" in whose midst the LORD rejoices (3:14-17).

sections.h: Words for God's anger in Zephaniah
sections.b: Zephaniah uses five words for God's anger and keeps them apart in the Plain: 'evrah "fury" (1:15, 18), charon 'af "burning anger" (2:2; 3:8), 'af "anger" (2:2-3), za'am "indignation" (3:8) and qin'ah "jealousy" (1:18; 3:8). The jealousy is the fierce loyalty of a spouse, set burning by the worship of other gods (1:4-6).

Genesis 11:1-9 says the whole earth had "one lip" until the LORD confused their lips at Babel. Zephaniah 3:9 promises that he will change the peoples' lips into pure lips, so that all call on his name. Christians read this with Pentecost (Acts 2:1-11). Readers differ on whether it means cleansed speech or one speech again. The verse itself names no language.

Zephaniah 1:6 names those who never sought the LORD or inquired of him. Zephaniah 2:3 calls the humble to "seek the LORD, seek righteousness, seek humility" and adds "perhaps you will be hidden on the day of the LORD's anger." The verbs are baqash (seek) and darash (inquire).

Zephaniah 3:14-20 is one of the longest passages addressed to Daughter Zion. She is told to cry out, shout and celebrate because the LORD has removed her judgments, the King of Israel is in her midst, and he will quiet his love and cheer over her. The Greek of 3:14 begins "Rejoice," the same word as Gabriel's greeting in Luke 1:28.

Zephaniah is the ninth of the Twelve in both the Hebrew and the Greek order. Links with its neighbors: "Hush before the Lord GOD" (1:7) and Habakkuk 2:20; "the day of the LORD" with Joel and Amos; the fall of Nineveh (2:13-15) with Nahum and Jonah; the humble remnant (3:12-13) with Micah 5 and Zechariah; and the reversal of fortunes (3:20) with the whole Twelve's hope.

sections.b: Zephaniah 2:4-15 aims one oracle at each compass point: the Philistines to the west, Moab and Ammon to the east, Cush to the south, Assyria to the north. The ring echoes Amos 1-2. Chapter 3 then turns the same judgment on Jerusalem itself.

sections.h: Calling on the LORD's name: Zephaniah 3:9
sections.b: Zephaniah 3:9 says God will give the peoples pure lips so that all of them call on the LORD's name and serve him side by side. Joel 2:32 says everyone who calls on his name will be saved; Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 quote it. The churches differ on how far and by what means this reaches those who have not heard the gospel: see the card on Zephaniah 3:9.

In the Greek, Zephaniah 3:14-17 begins "Rejoice" (chaire), and says the Lord is "in your midst" (3:15, 3:17). Only the first word, chaire, is the same as Gabriel's greeting in Luke 1:28; "Do not be afraid" (Luke 1:30) matches the Hebrew of 3:16, not the Greek, which reads "Take courage" (tharsei). Catholic teaching calls Mary the "Daughter of Sion" (Lumen Gentium 55, which does not cite Zephaniah), and the Roman lectionary reads Zephaniah 3:14-18 at the Visitation and on the Third Sunday of Advent in Year C. Other traditions are not cited here. See the card on Zephaniah 3:14-17.

Zephaniah uses the word gibbor, "warrior," twice. In 1:14 a warrior shouts in the day of the LORD. In 3:17 the LORD himself is "a warrior who rescues." The same war language that frightens in chapter 1 comforts in chapter 3.

Zephaniah 1:2-3 lists people, animals, birds and fish in the reverse of the order in Genesis 1:20-27, and uses the flood's wording, "off the surface of the ground." Judgment is creation undone. The book ends with a new beginning: pure lips (3:9) and a humble remnant (3:12-13).

Zephaniah 1:18 and 3:8 both say that "the whole earth" will be eaten up in the fire of God's jealousy. Readers differ: it is a sweeping picture of the fall of Judah (preterist), a picture of the last judgment (futurist and many traditional readings), or both. 2 Peter 3:7-12 speaks of the day of the Lord with fire in similar language.

Zephaniah's family is traced four generations to a "Hezekiah." Some interpreters identify him with King Hezekiah (about 715 to 686 BC), which would make Zephaniah a relative of Josiah. The Hebrew does not say "king," so others think it is another man of that name.
